channel.title: THE LEXICON
channel.description: A research archive mapping fashion history, visual culture, and the lineage of ideas. 45 landmark collections annotated by analytical category, designer, era, and movement.

item.title: Alexander McQueen SS 1999 — THE LEXICON
item.description: McQueen sent a Paralympic athlete down the runway on carved wooden legs, then had robots spray-paint a dress live. It made people ask what a 'perfect' body is.

item.title: Thierry Mugler AW 1995 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Thierry Mugler threw a huge show in a Paris circus building with a hundred outfits and the most famous models of the day. Its robot suits, corsets and latex made it one of the most extreme shows ever staged.

item.title: Issey Miyake SS 1999 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Issey Miyake showed clothes cut from one long tube of machine-knitted fabric, so you could snip out a dress with no sewing. It imagined a smarter, less wasteful way of making clothes.

item.title: Balenciaga SS 2007 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Nicolas Ghesquière sent out models in shiny gold leggings and metal legs that looked like robot parts. It mixed fashion with sci-fi and asked where the human body ends and the machine begins.

item.title: Hussein Chalayan AW 2000 — THE LEXICON
item.description: In a living-room set, models took the covers off chairs and wore them as dresses, and a wooden table turned into a skirt. It was about refugees who must carry their home with them when they flee.

item.title: Prada SS 1996 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Miuccia Prada used 'ugly' colours and prints that clashed on purpose, inspired by everyday objects. It became known as 'ugly chic' and proved bad taste could be smart and stylish.

item.title: John Galliano for Dior Couture SS 2000 — THE LEXICON
item.description: John Galliano based a Dior couture show on people living rough by the river in Paris, with torn and layered clothes. It caused anger, and it still raises the question of whether fashion should borrow from poverty.

item.title: Rick Owens SS 2014 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Instead of models, Rick Owens cast forty step dancers, from a dance style born in Black American colleges, who stomped down the runway pulling fierce faces. It challenged who gets to show clothes, and how.

item.title: Comme des Garçons SS 1997 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Rei Kawakubo put padded lumps on the back, hips and shoulders of stretchy dresses, changing the shape of the body. The press nicknamed it 'lumps and bumps', but it made people rethink what a 'beautiful' figure is.

item.title: Yohji Yamamoto AW 1998 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Yohji Yamamoto mixed old-fashioned shapes with stretchy knits, including a model leaping down the runway in a ball-shaped skirt and a giant wedding-dress finale. It made clothes that move against the body, not just with it.

item.title: Jean Paul Gaultier SS 1994 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Jean Paul Gaultier printed tattoo designs onto see-through mesh tops, so models looked tattooed from head to toe. It brought tattoo and body-piercing culture onto the runway long before it went mainstream.

item.title: Viktor & Rolf AW 1999 — THE LEXICON
item.description: One model stood on a turning platform while the designers put nine outfits on her, one over another, like a Russian doll. It turned dressing itself into the show.

item.title: Helmut Lang AW 1998 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Helmut Lang cancelled his New York show and put the collection online and on CD-ROM instead, the first designer to do so. Today every brand streams its shows, and this is where that started.

item.title: Moschino AW 2014 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Jeremy Scott turned McDonald's uniforms and junk-food packaging into luxury clothes. It was a joke about how fashion copies cheap, fast culture, and it made people ask what 'luxury' even means.

item.title: Schiaparelli Haute Couture SS 2021 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Shown in a short film during lockdown, Daniel Roseberry's couture had moulded tops shaped like muscly chests and bodies cast in gold. It played with how surreal and theatrical fashion can be.

item.title: Maison Martin Margiela AW 2000 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Martin Margiela made women's clothes in giant men's sizes, so models seemed to swim inside them. It mocked fashion's obsession with fit and size, and oversized clothes have been everywhere ever since.

item.title: Vivienne Westwood AW 1981 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Vivienne Westwood's first catwalk show dressed models as pirates in loose shirts, sashes and wide trousers. It turned the dressing-up style of London's club kids into fashion and ended her punk era.

item.title: Raf Simons AW 2001 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Raf Simons's models marched in hoods and huge layered jackets covered in graphics, to loud techno music. It became the blueprint for the big, graphic streetwear that luxury brands still sell today.

item.title: Undercover SS 2003 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Jun Takahashi stitched scraps of fabric over one another to look like healing scabs on the skin. It turned something gross into something beautiful and brought Japanese street style to Paris.

item.title: Miguel Adrover AW 2000 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Miguel Adrover held an underground show in New York using old, thrown-away clothes, including a coat made from his late neighbour's stained mattress. It made people ask who decides what counts as luxury, and what counts as rubbish.

item.title: Iris van Herpen AW 2011 Couture — THE LEXICON
item.description: Iris van Herpen showed a 3D-printed dress shaped like a skeleton worn outside the body. It was an early sign of how computers and new technology would change the way clothes are made.

item.title: Gareth Pugh AW 2006 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Gareth Pugh showed black and white outfits made of inflated plastic balloons and sharp geometric shapes. It looked more like a performance-art piece than a fashion show and made him a star of London fashion.

item.title: Vetements AW 2015 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Vetements took everyday things like a DHL delivery-company T-shirt and sold them as high fashion. It made people laugh, argue and ask whether copying the ordinary can be clever design.

item.title: Hood By Air SS 2014 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Shayne Oliver brought New York's underground club and queer scene to the runway with bold logo T-shirts and streetwear. It helped make streetwear a serious part of high fashion.

item.title: Junya Watanabe AW 2015 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Junya Watanabe built clothes from folded pyramid shapes, like paper lanterns or origami, using careful maths to plan each fold. It showed how geometry can turn flat fabric into sculpture.

item.title: Craig Green SS 2015 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Craig Green's models walked barefoot carrying wooden frames like kites and sails tied to their bodies. The show was so moving that some people in the audience cried, and it made his name overnight.

item.title: Gucci AW 2018 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Alessandro Michele set his Gucci show in an operating theatre, with models carrying lifelike copies of their own heads. It asked how technology and surgery are changing what it means to have a body.

item.title: Thom Browne AW 2012 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Thom Browne turned the New York Public Library into a dreamlike set where models stepped out of wooden coffins in dark veils and grey suits. It took the office suit and made it strange and ghostly.

item.title: Loewe SS 2023 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Jonathan Anderson made dresses with real-looking flowers growing out of them and tops that looked like pixelated screenshots. It made clothes look like surreal sculptures and joked about life seen through screens.

item.title: Marine Serre SS 2020 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Marine Serre held a show in the rain about climate disaster, and made about half the clothes from old, recycled materials. It showed that waste can be turned into luxury fashion.

item.title: Chanel AW 2014 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Karl Lagerfeld turned a Paris exhibition hall into a giant supermarket filled with Chanel-branded groceries. It was a joke about shopping and about how luxury brands sell their name on everything.

item.title: Louis Vuitton SS 2008 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Marc Jacobs showed the collection in the round at the Louvre, with clothes made for women always travelling. It showed how a heritage luggage brand used art and celebrity to become the world's biggest luxury label.

item.title: Celine SS 2010 — THE LEXICON
item.description: After five years away, Phoebe Philo returned with plain, beautifully cut clothes and no decoration at all. It was a quiet show that changed what grown-up, modern fashion looked like for the next ten years.

item.title: Valentino AW 2022 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Pierpaolo Piccioli dressed almost the whole show in one shade of hot pink, which he had made into its own official colour. Pink took over fashion and red carpets for the next year.

item.title: Miu Miu SS 2022 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Miuccia Prada showed tiny low-rise skirts with cropped tops cut to bare the stomach. The look was copied across the world, and it is one of the clearest examples of a runway outfit going viral.

item.title: Calvin Klein 205W39NYC AW 2017 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Raf Simons filled Calvin Klein's New York show with American flags, cowboy fringe and horror-film references. It looked at America's own pop culture as something both glamorous and frightening.

item.title: Givenchy AW 2015 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Riccardo Tisci mixed church-style lace and embroidery with face jewellery and sportswear, showing in a glass-and-steel business district. It blended the holy and the edgy into one dark, glamorous look.

item.title: Dries Van Noten SS 2015 — THE LEXICON
item.description: For his 100th show, Dries Van Noten layered rich prints, painted silks and velvet, after a dinner for the people who had worked with him for years. It celebrated slow, long-term craft in a fast industry.

item.title: Saint Laurent AW 2013 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Hedi Slimane showed grungy slip dresses, plaid shirts and leather jackets inspired by young rock fans in California. Critics argued about whether a famous Paris fashion house should look this much like the street.

item.title: Coperni SS 2023 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Bella Hadid walked on stage almost bare and a liquid dress was sprayed onto her body in front of the audience. It went viral because it was made to be filmed, not photographed.

item.title: Haider Ackermann AW 2014 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Haider Ackermann made clothes that seem to twist around the body, with seams running on the diagonal and deep reds, greys and golds. It showed how cut and fabric alone, with no logos or tricks, can feel powerful.

item.title: Bottega Veneta AW 2019 — THE LEXICON
item.description: In his first show, Daniel Lee made the brand's woven leather huge and bold, with no logo in sight. His soft Pouch bag became one of the most copied accessories of the next two years.

item.title: Jil Sander SS 2011 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Raf Simons took the shapes of 1950s couture gowns and made them in loud, bright colour blocks with T-shirts. It mixed old-fashioned elegance with something fresh and almost sporty.

item.title: Chromat SS 2020 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Chromat put people of every size, age, ability and gender on the runway in sporty swimwear and stretch clothes. It pushed fashion shows to include all kinds of bodies, not just the usual model sizes.

item.title: JW Anderson AW 2022 — THE LEXICON
item.description: Jonathan Anderson showed huge, oddly shaped knits and clothes that seem to sit in the wrong place on the body. It played with what we expect clothes to look like, and his pieces spread fast online.
